title: Distinguish process-wide access from a container registration lifetime and account for concurrency, disposal, and hidden global dependencies

questions.prompt:
An ASP.NET Core app registers `services.AddSingleton<IClock, Clock>()`. While registration is still running, a helper method calls `services.BuildServiceProvider()` and resolves `IClock` from it to configure another option. Later, the app resolves `IClock` from its normal application provider. Logging shows that two different `Clock` instances were created.

Which explanation is correct?
options: `AddSingleton` keeps one instance per thread, so the startup thread running the helper received its own `Clock`.
Singleton instances are created per scope, and the helper resolved outside any scope, so the first request scope created a new `Clock`.
Each `BuildServiceProvider` call creates a separate root provider with its own singleton cache, and singleton lifetime only applies within one root provider.
The container disposes and recreates all singletons when registration finishes, so the startup `Clock` was replaced by a new one.

rubric.point: Chooses the option saying each `BuildServiceProvider` call creates a separate root provider with its own singleton set.

questions.model: **Option 3.** `AddSingleton` means one instance per root provider and registration, not one per process. Calling `BuildServiceProvider` during registration creates a second container, which has its own singleton cache, so it creates a second `Clock`.

questions.prompt:
A web API registers `RequestCounter` with `services.AddSingleton<RequestCounter>()`. The class has a plain `Dictionary<string, int>` field. Every incoming request calls a method that increments the count for the caller's API key, with no locking. A developer says: "This is safe because the .NET DI container is thread-safe."

Explain why this reasoning is wrong.

rubric.point: Explains that the container's thread safety covers creating and resolving the service, not the instance's own fields or dependencies.
Explains that one shared instance serves concurrent requests, so unsynchronized updates to the dictionary can race and corrupt the counts or the dictionary.

questions.model:
The container only guarantees that creating and resolving the service is thread-safe. It does nothing to protect the object's state. Because the service is a singleton, every concurrent request uses the same `RequestCounter`, so unlocked increments on the shared `Dictionary` can race, losing updates or corrupting the dictionary.

*Optional:* the whole read–modify–write increment must be atomic. Either take a lock around the entire increment, or use `ConcurrentDictionary.AddOrUpdate(key, 1, (_, n) => n + 1)`. Swapping in `ConcurrentDictionary` but keeping `counts[key]++` still loses updates, because the read and the write are separate operations.
